definition: Everything that keeps aircraft safely separated and flowing smoothly: controllers, rules, and the equipment they rely on.
Communication, Navigation and Surveillance: the three families of equipment behind air traffic management.
How pilots and controllers talk to each other, by voice radio or by text messages over a data link.
How an aircraft knows where it is and which way to go.
How controllers on the ground see where aircraft are.
The service of controllers who give pilots instructions to keep aircraft apart.
A person on the ground who watches traffic on a screen and gives pilots instructions.
The International Civil Aviation Organization, the United Nations agency that writes worldwide aviation standards.
The ICAO rulebook for aeronautical radio: it sets the frequencies, signals and performance of CNS equipment.
Air Traffic Safety Electronics Personnel: the engineers and technicians who install, maintain and certify CNS equipment.
An invisible wave of electric and magnetic energy that travels at the speed of light. Radios, radars and satellites all use them.
About 300,000 km per second. Radio waves travel at this speed, so one nautical mile takes about 6 millionths of a second.
How many times a wave wiggles each second, measured in hertz (Hz). Different systems use different frequencies so they do not interfere.
One cycle per second. A kilohertz (kHz) is a thousand, a megahertz (MHz) a million, a gigahertz (GHz) a billion.
The distance from one wave crest to the next. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength.
A metal structure that turns electrical signals into radio waves, or catches radio waves and turns them back into signals.
The part of a radio system that creates and sends out the signal.
The part of a radio system that picks up a signal and extracts its information.
A clear straight path between two antennas. Most aviation radio needs it: hills and the curve of the Earth block the signal.
The farthest distance a radio signal can reach before the curve of the Earth gets in the way. Higher antennas see farther.
One millionth of a second. Radio signals cross about 300 metres in one microsecond.
The distance unit of aviation and shipping: 1,852 metres, about 1.15 ordinary miles.
One nautical mile per hour, the speed unit of aviation. 250 kt is about 460 km/h.
Altitude in hundreds of feet using a standard pressure setting. FL350 means about 35,000 feet.
Height above mean sea level, measured in feet in aviation.
The straight diagonal distance from a ground station up to an aircraft, not the distance along the ground.
A direction measured in degrees clockwise from north: 090 is east, 180 is south, 270 is west.
The direction the aircraft's nose is pointing, in degrees from north.
The direction to the geographic North Pole, the top of a map.
The direction a compass needle points. It is a few degrees away from true north in most places.
The angle between true north and magnetic north at a place. Aviation directions are usually given relative to magnetic north.
The direction of something measured clockwise from the aircraft's nose: 000 is straight ahead, 090 off the right wing.
A line going outward from a radio station in a given magnetic direction. Flying on the 090 radial means you are east of the station.
Where a wave is in its cycle at a given moment. Two waves can have the same rhythm but be shifted in time: that shift is the phase difference.
The change in frequency you notice when a sound source moves toward or away from you, like a passing siren. Radio waves do the same.
Adding information to a radio wave by changing its strength, frequency or timing.
Carrying information by making a radio wave stronger and weaker.
Carrying information by shifting a radio wave's frequency slightly up and down.
The main radio wave that is sent out and then modulated to carry information.
A very short burst of radio energy, often less than a millionth of a second long.
A way of comparing signal strengths on a scale where every 10 dB is ten times more power.
How much weaker a radio signal gets as it spreads out over distance.
How much stronger the wanted signal is than the background hiss. Too low, and the receiver cannot pick it out.
A screen that draws a signal as a wave over time, so you can see its shape and timing.
A picture of a signal by frequency: which frequencies are present and how strong each one is.
A dial or display in front of the pilot that shows information such as direction, distance or course.
A cockpit instrument whose vertical needle shows whether the aircraft is left or right of the chosen course.
The knob on a CDI that lets the pilot choose which course to follow.
An indicator on the CDI that says whether the chosen course leads toward the station or away from it.
A CDI combined with a compass card, so the pilot sees the course and the heading together.
An aircraft receiver whose needle points toward an NDB radio station.
An instrument with a compass card that turns with the aircraft's heading and a needle pointing at a station, so the pilot reads the magnetic bearing directly.
The classic round radar screen: the radar is in the centre, north is up, and echoes appear at their direction and distance.
The rotating line on a radar screen that shows where the antenna is pointing right now.
A spot of light on a radar screen made by an echo.
A simple ground radio transmitter that sends the same signal in all directions, so aircraft can point at it.
VHF omnidirectional range: a ground station that tells an aircraft which direction (radial) it is from the station.
A ground station that answers an aircraft's radio question so the aircraft can measure its distance to the station.
Two radio beams at the runway that guide an aircraft left-right and up-down down to the runway in bad weather.
Global Navigation Satellite System: GPS, Galileo, GLONASS or BeiDou. Satellites broadcast time signals that let a receiver work out its position.
Radio detection and ranging: finding objects by sending radio energy and listening for what comes back.
A radio box in the aircraft that automatically answers when a secondary radar asks, replying with an identity code and altitude.
The four-digit code (digits 0 to 7) a controller gives a pilot to set on the transponder, so that aircraft can be identified on the screen.
Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast: the aircraft works out its own position by satellite and broadcasts it to anyone listening.
Megahertz: a million cycles per second. VHF radio is around 118 to 137 MHz.
Very high frequency, 30 to 300 MHz. Used for aviation voice radio, VOR and ILS. It travels in straight lines.
Ultra high frequency, 300 MHz to 3 GHz. Used by DME, secondary radar, GNSS and military radio.
High frequency, 3 to 30 MHz. These waves can bounce off the upper atmosphere and travel thousands of kilometres.
Having more than one way to do something, so that one failure does not stop the whole system.
